transcript:
Header:
- Date/Time: 2027-05-04 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 45 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lina (Nebula Product), Rahul (Nebula Lead Eng), Samir (Nebula Infra), Asha (Nebula Security)

Summary: quick sync on app integration; focus on SDK examples for function and tool calls, how to produce stable structured JSON from model output, and perf/security next steps.

00:00 - 00:22 Maya: thanks everyone for joining, uh, quick agenda — SDK patterns, structured output examples, errors Rahul hit in staging, and perf/security follow ups.
00:23 - 00:47 Lina: sounds good — we pushed the new integration into staging, saw a mix of good/garbled outputs when we call the function handlers.
00:48 - 01:10 Ethan: can you describe the garbled outputs — is it schema mismatch or partial responses?
01:11 - 01:37 Rahul: mostly partial JSON, like closed braces missing, or sometimes keys renamed, e.g., `patient_id` becomes `patient id` or `patientId` different casing; also some stream truncation at ~512 tokens.
01:38 - 02:05 Maya: ok yeah that's classic model-output variance — two approaches we recommend: 1) use the SDK's function-calling abstraction so the model returns a structured payload, or 2) post-validate with a small schema parser and fallback to a heuristic re-call. we'll show examples.
02:06 - 02:42 Ethan: note that our function-call wrapper enforces a shape and uses a deterministic generation mode for structured outputs; in Node/Python SDK we include an example `parse_and_validate()` helper. i'll add a sample that matches your clinical-note schema.
02:43 - 03:10 Lina: perfect. also, when you say deterministic do you mean temperature zero? we tried temp 0.2 and still saw differences.
03:11 - 03:36 Ethan: temperature helps but there are still model-specific quirks. function-calling plus explicit schema constraints reduces cost because you avoid repeated retries. the SDK also supports a `require_keys` option that prompts the model to always include top-level fields.
03:37 - 04:05 Rahul: we also hit a few 502s during heavy batch testing (around 200 req/s). Samir dug into logs — looks like some backend worker OOMs when kv-cache spikes with long contexts.
04:06 - 04:30 Samir: yes logs show GC spikes, and some requests fall back to smaller model variants which then produce different output shapes. we need to avoid fallback for these calls if possible.
04:31 - 05:00 Maya: that's exactly where dedicated pools help — you can pin model variant and kernel optimizations. we can also tune batching window and KV cache eviction for your workload. we'll run a perf test on a Dedicated pool to reproduce.
05:01 - 05:34 Ethan: quick note — we observed that continuous batching with max latency 120ms cut token cost by ~20% on similar EHR workloads; but with very long contexts we recommend bumping memory and using quantized kernels.
05:35 - 06:03 Lina: thanks. on structured output: our downstream systems need a strict JSON schema for clinical notes: sections, section timestamps, diagnosis codes, free-text summary. we'll share their schema.
06:04 - 06:30 Maya: great, if you share schema we'll convert to an SDK example with `function_schema` and an example prompt template.
06:31 - 07:02 Rahul: another integration quirk — when we do tool-calls (we call an internal RLS tool to fetch demographics) the SDK function-call flow and our tool call are sometimes racing, result is duplication. any best practice?
07:03 - 07:36 Ethan: yes, we recommend serializing external tool calls inside the function wrapper: i.e., model asks for a tool, SDK performs tool, returns tool result in the same function call payload back to model, then model completes structured output. prevents races. we'll include sample patterns.
07:37 - 08:05 Lina: could you show an example of that in Python? our backend is mostly Python.
08:06 - 09:00 Ethan: (brief code walkthrough) so you `register_tool('get_demographics')` then in the function handler you call your internal API, return the JSON, and Redwood's SDK will send that back as `tool_result` in the following model invocation. important to set `stream=false` for those flows to avoid partials.
09:01 - 09:35 Lina: stream=false might increase latency, though, any mitigations?
09:36 - 10:02 Ethan: tradeoff — streaming helps UX but for strict schema produce you want atomic responses. alternative: stream tokens for the human-readable summary while the structured part is produced by a separate non-streamed invocation.
10:03 - 11:00 Rahul: about perf — Samir ran a quick Dedicated sim and saw the OOMs around 12k tokens. what's Redwood's recommendation for 16k contexts?
11:01 - 11:28 Maya: for 16k we recommend 80GB+ GPU variants and aggressive KV eviction policy; also use quantized kernels and pin model variant to avoid fallback. we'll run a controlled perf test and give QPS/latency numbers.
11:29 - 12:00 Samir: can you also include cost estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted with our expected traffic (1.2M tokens/day)?
12:01 - 12:26 Maya: yes we'll include a comparative estimate — Dedicated committed pricing vs Hosted per-token; and we'll include batching suggestions to hit cost targets.
12:27 - 12:59 Asha: quick security note — we require KMS integration and audit trails; sample logs of model input/ outputs must be redact-capable. also SOC 2 compliance evidence.
13:00 - 13:25 Maya: understood — Redwood supports customer-managed KMS and configurable audit retention; we'll bring security docs and schedule a deep-dive with your security team.
13:26 - 14:05 Rahul: back to integration errors — i'll paste two sample failing requests and the corresponding logs into the shared Confluence page after this meeting.
14:06 - 14:40 Ethan: thanks — once we have the logs we can correlate with worker OOMs and batching windows. we might recommend reducing max batch size for the endpoints that use very long contexts.
14:41 - 15:20 Lina: one small ask — could you include an example of structured output with both free-text summary and discrete fields so our downstream can choose?
15:21 - 16:05 Maya: yes — we'll include two patterns: unified JSON (all fields + freeText) and split flow (one call for structured fields and a second for narrative summary). pros/cons in the doc.
16:06 - 17:00 Rahul: any blockers on our side to get the SDK update? we can deploy immediately once we have the sample.
17:01 - 17:28 Ethan: no blockers; i'll push a branch with samples and a short test harness that mimics your tool call to reproduce locally.
17:29 - 18:00 Samir: do you have sample deck we can share with execs that shows latency/cost tradeoffs?
18:01 - 18:28 Maya: yes a one-pager — we'll drop that in the shared folder.
18:29 - 20:00 (brief silence while links are pasted into chat)
20:01 - 21:00 Maya: recap & next steps — Ethan to update SDK samples, Maya to share structured output schema examples and cost deck, Samir/Rahul to provide failing logs, Asha to schedule security deep-dive.
21:01 - 22:00 Lina: thanks everyone — feeling good about direction.
22:01 - 22:30 Maya: ok we'll follow up in slack and set security call. thanks all.

Notes (imperfect transcript): occasional mis-hearings — 'kv cache' spelled K-V cache in logs, `Redwood Dedicated` heard as `Redwood Delicated` in a few spots. timestamps are approximate.

End of transcript.
